newsitem.title: USA: Florida rejects penny tax on sugar producers.
newsitem.headline: Florida rejects penny tax on sugar producers.

text.p: Florida voters soured on a proposed $900 million tax on sugar growers while overwhelmingly passing a measure that will make it more difficult for voters to pass future tax proposals.

With 75 percent of the votes counted early Wednesday, 54 percent of Floridians appeared ready to reject a 1 cent a pound tax on sugar grown in the Everglades, marking the end of a bitterly fought campaign pitting well-heeled campaigns on both sides of the issue.
In an added blow to sugar tax supporters, voters on Tuesday approved a related amendment to require a two-thirds vote for any new tax proposal.
Sponsored by the Tax Cap Committee, Amendment 1 was heavily financed by the sugar industry in an effort to insulate itself if the sugar tax passed. More than 69 percent of Floridians agreed.

Environmentalists and sugar producers spent an estimated $36 million in a flurry of radio, television and newspaper advertisements. It was the second-most expensive ballot initiative in U.S. history, according to experts.
A loan of nearly $3 million from commodities trader Paul Tudor Jones helped the environmentalists keep their campaign going in the final weeks. Tudor is a part-time resident of the Florida Keys.
Shortly before 11 p.m. EST, the sugar industry declared victory, saying Florida voters "had spoken loud and clear."

"I and the other sugar farmers are committed to Everglades restoration and we pledge to do our fair share in finishing the job of ensuring that the Everglades ecosystem is preserved forever,'' said J. Nelson Fairbanks, president and CEO of U.S. Sugar Corp. in a prepared statement.

Sugar tax backers, led by the Miami-based organization, Save Our Everglades, reluctantly declared defeat on Amendment 4, but added that they were thankful that two related ballot proposals were approved. The measures will create a trust fund to pay for Everglades clean-up, and will require those who cause the pollution to help shoulder the estimated $1.7 billion cost of restoration.
"It's a little bittersweet," said Mary Barley, head of Save Our Everglades.
But she added, "This is a clear electoral mandate to the governor and legislature to immediately present the sugar industry with a $1 billion bill to clean up their pollution."

Tuesday's vote was a pivotal event in the ongoing battle between sugar companies and environmental groups over Everglades clean-up. With the passage of Amendment 1, the industry is less likely to face another vote on the issue.
"Money is power," said Tax Cap organizer Kate Zichella of Naples. "The people have to control the flow of money if the people are to retain the power."
